extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political history and theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes standards, institutional rules, and normative judgments about laws and constitutional arrangements found in a historical account of ancient Greek and Roman republican institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orders and balances (balanced government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders and balances existed in his institution (Charondas); the legislator examined laws and established orders and balances to regulate the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats 'orders and balances' as essential to stable government; their existence is asserted though Charondas' laws are lost. The author implies that lack of known institutional balances leads to instability and dissolution of democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public education in reading and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: He ordained that all the Cons of every family should learn to write and read under masters in the pay of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises this law as of such merit that it 'deserves to be imitated by every free people at least'; public funding of basic education is presented as a foundation for civic life and civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion from public councils for remarried fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: He excluded from all his public councils all men who, having children, should marry a second time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale given: to prevent a stepmother from mortifying (harassing) children. This is an example of a moral/social rule tied to office-holding eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public shaming punishment for calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: All who should be convicted of calumny should be conducted through the streets crowned with tamarin, a punishment so infamous that several put an end to their own lives rather than submit to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe public humiliation is used as a deterrent against slander; the account notes its extreme severity and effectiveness in deterring calumny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on association with wicked men
rubrics_metrics.description: He prohibited all society with wicked men: 'the disposition to evil is very strong; and many of those who at first love virtue are often drawn in ... to the greatest vices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as preventive moral legislation meant to reduce contagion of vice by restricting social association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of guardianship of orphans by parental line
rubrics_metrics.description: That the property of orphans should be administered by the relations by the father, but their persons and education entrusted to those by the mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific rule for guardianship and property administration aimed at protecting both property and upbringing; an example of detailed family-law regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative punishments for cowardice (social humiliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: All those who should refuse to take arms for their country, or quit their ranks in the army, instead of being punished by death, should be exposed three days in a public square of the city in women's clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a non-lethal but stigmatizing punishment for military cowardice—social humiliation as a civic sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the law's letter over individual eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: He reprehended and silenced all criminals who substituted turns of eloquence and arbitrary interpretations in place of the letter of the laws, and charged them with violating their authority and majesty. 'Whether you shall save the law or the criminal?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: the literal application and authority of law must be preserved against rhetorical or arbitrary reinterpretation; legal stability over individual exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe procedural restrictions on proposing legal changes
rubrics_metrics.description: He ordained that no citizen should present himself in the public assembly to propose any reformation or alteration in the law without an halter about his neck, which he should wear till the people had deliberated and determined; if the people decreed the proposed alteration hurtful or unnecessary, the reformer should be strangled on the spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An extreme procedural barrier to legal innovation intended to prevent factional seditions and preserve constitutional stability; author notes it 'silenced all new legislators' and allowed only three changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of laws by comparative study and practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Charondas, having examined to the foundation the laws of all countries, chose out of them, for his country, the wisest and most convenient. Some others he added, drawn from his own meditations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation grounded in comparative legal study and practical selection of the best rules; recommends borrowing and adapting proven institutions rather than inventing arbitrarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation of law on piety and rational philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Zaleucus' preamble: inhabitants ought to be persuaded there is a God; by contemplating the heavens they will see order not chance; they should adore the gods and hold their souls pure because gods accept only the just and beneficent actions of virtuous men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that laws should appeal to religious belief and rational moral philosophy as the motive for civic obedience; positions piety and wisdom as the basis for durable laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of reconciliation and impartial magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: He ordained that there should never be among them any irreconcileable enmity; animosities should be only a passage to sure and sincere reconciliation; chiefs ought not to govern with arrogance nor pride; magistrates should not be guided by hatred or by friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norms for civic culture and magistrate conduct: moderation, reconciliation, and impartiality are presented as constitutional virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and balance of powers (veto/negative for executive)
rubrics_metrics.description: It would have been necessary to give the consuls, or one of them, the executive power, and a negative both upon the senate and popular assembly in the legislature; making the senate and people equal and independent would have preserved the republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that an effective republican constitution requires distinct, balanced branches with mutual checks (including an executive veto) to prevent dominance by one order and preserve liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of productive civic occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: By the institution of Horatius the Roman people, even the lowest class, were directed to apply themselves to pasturage, agriculture, and mechanic arts; this had the natural effect of producing a numerous, hardy, courageous people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic policy that encourages agriculture and trades is praised as creating stable, industrious citizens less susceptible to tyranny and demagoguery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative institutions must have substantive powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunes, authorized only to forbid measures, not to propose laws, were insufficient; a representative assembly would have an equal right with the senate to propose laws, deliberate, debate, alter, amend, improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes institutions that give the people's representatives only negative powers; effective representation requires positive legislative authority to redress grievances and balance aristocratic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional protections for popular magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunes' persons were made sacred and protected from violence; laws forbade interruption while a tribune spoke under pain of death or fine, and they were eventually elected by tribes to avoid patrician control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protecting representatives (sacred status, election procedures) is necessary to allow them to defend popular rights against aristocratic interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification of laws for clarity and legal procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The decemvirs presented a number of laws, engraved on ten tables (later Twelve Tables), containing privileges of the people, crimes to be punished, and forms of judicial proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codified statutes and formal judicial procedures create certainty and security necessary for commerce, arts, and liberties; but codification may also enshrine harsh provisions if not tempered by justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessively harsh penal provisions (e.g., for bankruptcy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Twelve Tables bankruptcy was made a crime and exposed the insolvent debtor to the mercy of his creditors, who might put him to death, divide his members, etc.; the law shows atrocious ideas and manners of the age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes cruel provisions and implies that codified law must be humane; clarity is good, but harsh substantive rules undermine justice and social stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on paternal power
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving to fathers the power of magistrates, or the power of life and death over their children, is criticized as indefensible despite alleged reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family law and paternal authority should be constrained; extreme paternal powers are morally and politically problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of unlimited power in temporary committees
rubrics_metrics.description: The decemvirs were intended as a committee to prepare a draft but were vested with temporary sovereignty and unlimited power over lives and fortunes, leading to abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary principle: delegating wide, unchecked sovereign power even temporarily invites tyranny; institutional limits and ongoing accountability are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty and publicity of law as prerequisite for prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only under the security of certain and known laws that arts, sciences, agriculture, commerce, and trades can ever be made to flourish; law uncertain and unknown is 'miserable servitude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable, public, and intelligible laws are necessary for economic and cultural development; uncertainty in law produces servitude and undermines national happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable distribution of land to address popular grievances (agrarian reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agrarian law (equal division of land) arose as a popular demand to remedy lands passing into powerful citizens' hands rather than being divided equally among the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redistributive land measures are presented as legitimate popular responses to elite capture of conquered lands; agrarian reform is framed as a political tool to address inequality and avert unrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid entwining judiciary and aristocratic discretionary power
rubrics_metrics.description: The patricians' discretionary judicial powers supported their dominance; the people's effort to compile a body of laws (Twelve Tables) sought to regulate judicial forms and constrain patrician discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalizing judicial procedure and limiting arbitrary discretion is necessary to curb aristocratic domination, but must be balanced so as not to undermine other constitutional checks.
